text: This is a walkthrough of version one. What you're seeing is a wireframe. It shows what each screen does and how the work moves through it, not the final look. We'll follow one job, from the first estimate to the paid invoice.

A customer calls about wrapping two vans. The owner starts an estimate and adds each van from a saved package. One click pulls in every line: the film, laminate, ink, design time, and installation, with cost, price, and margin on each.
Inside the shop, the estimate stays itemized. Switch to the customer view, and each van becomes a single line with one price. Same estimate, two audiences.
The customer approves one van now, and holds off on the second. The system records who approved, when, and how. Then a deposit link goes out by email, and the customer pays it by card.
Approving the work creates the job. It lands on the job board, where every active job moves through its stages. When printing starts, the owner drags it into production.

Now the technician's side, on a phone. Technicians only see the jobs assigned to them, and never see prices or costs. They punch in for the day, open the job, and start a timer. Only one timer runs at a time, so hours can't be counted twice. When the install is done, they add completion photos and send it back for review.
Back at the desk, the job is waiting for review. The owner checks the photos, sees estimated against actual hours, and closes the job. Closing it creates the draft invoice.

One line per vehicle, the deposit already taken off, and the customer's other unpaid invoices listed underneath. The owner sends it with a payment link. The customer pays by card, the balance updates on its own, and it all flows through to QuickBooks.
At the end of the week, the owner reviews timesheets, approves them, and exports the hours for payroll. Daily punches and job time are kept separate, so nothing gets paid twice.

Graphics is the first division, but it's built on the same foundation the repair shops will move onto later. Each division sets its own words and its own stages. Graphics calls the work a job, and tracks production and installation. A mechanical shop can call it a service order, with repair stages instead. Same software, just configured differently.

And here's what version one does not include. Live inventory counts. A customer portal. The mechanical shops themselves. And anything that stays in GoHighLevel, like leads and texting. Those come later, built on top of this.
That's version one. Graphics runs completely off FullBay, on a foundation the rest of the company can grow into.
